scores.reason: Directly answers Q2 by decomposing which agentic moves carry the gain: recall quality, not search effort, predicts accuracy, and reformulation helps while redundant querying does not — mechanism-level attribution with a fixed retriever, exactly what C2 asks for.

The canonical answer to Q1: quantifies the single-query BM25 vs dense retriever recall gap (24.8% recall@5) on real literature-search queries, plus reranking gains (C3) and a documented benchmark-construction method (C4).

Fixed-corpus benchmark that explicitly disentangles retriever contribution from agent contribution, with quantified BM25 baseline (3.86%) vs dense retriever numbers — hits C1 and C4 squarely even though the domain is deep-research QA rather than lit search proper.

Survey/taxonomy with a genuine critique of benchmark limitations (metric misalignment, restricted knowledge access) relevant to Q3, but it quantifies nothing and attributes no gains — useful map, not decision-moving evidence.

The strongest C5 evidence in the list: shows per-query corpus curation inflated measured agentic performance, with recall collapsing from 84.3% to 21.4% on an uncurated corpus — exactly the premise-challenging result Q4 asks the scan to reach for.

Directly in the brief's domain with a detailed expert-labeled benchmark construction (ScholarQABench, C4) and quantified gains from a retrieval-plus-self-feedback design over plain LLMs, informing Q2 and Q3.

Agentic literature-retrieval system benchmarked against Google Scholar as a single-query baseline (C1) with the gain tied to intent-refinement and planning-retrieval separation (C2); key_finding is supported by the abstract, though the claimed mechanisms lack a visible ablation.

Isolates citation-graph traversal as the mechanism (C2) with a bounded, inspectable design that beats open-loop agents on LitSearch at lower cost — also usefully complicates the premise that open-ended agentic loops are what carries the gain.
Core prior work: quantifies agentic gain over Google/Google Scholar single-query baselines (recall@20/@50, C1+C2) and documents construction of both a synthetic and a real-query benchmark (C4).

Solid C3 evidence that embedding-retriever pipelines cap recall on reasoning-intensive queries and an alternative retrieval architecture, but it is general-purpose IR on BRIGHT, not attached to a literature-search agent or benchmark — relevant, not central.
